title: Not born, and never dying
theme: Yama begins to describe the self: the knower is not born and does not die; it came from nothing and nothing came from it; unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

sandhi.rule: A final t before n becomes n, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा); a + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
A final t before n becomes n, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा).
aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes o: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) with P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
aḥ before a becomes o and the a is elided (written with avagraha): P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) by extension and P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).
As above: aḥ → o before n, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

morphology.note: Present middle of jan, a ya-stem (class 4): ‘is born’. म्रियते, from mṛ ‘die’, is formed the same way and shares the negation.
Perfect 3 sg. of bhū ‘become, come to be’: ‘came into being’ — or, with कश्चित् as predicate, ‘became anyone’ (see Ambiguities).
Present passive participle of han ‘strike, slay’, in the locative with शरीरे: a locative absolute, ‘when the body is being slain’.
An old Vedic word for the inspired, the wise; here the self as knower. Śaṅkara explains why: its consciousness is never lost.

translation.literal: ‘The knower is not born or dies; this one came from nowhere; [nor] did anyone come to be [from it]. Unborn, eternal, everlasting [is] this ancient one; it is not slain when the body is slain.’
translation.readable: ‘The knowing self is never born and never dies. It did not come from anything, and nothing came from it. Unborn, eternal, lasting, ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.’

anvaya: विपश्चित् न जायते म्रियते वा । अयम् कुतश्चित् न बभूव । कश्चित् न बभूव । अयम् अजः नित्यः शाश्वतः पुराणः । शरीरे हन्यमाने न हन्यते ॥
syntax: Five short statements with one subject, vipaścit / ayam. The first two lines deny birth and death and any origin (na jāyate mriyate vā; nāyaṃ kutaścit na babhūva kaścit); four predicate adjectives follow (ajo nityaḥ śāśvato … purāṇaḥ); the verse ends with a locative absolute (hanyamāne śarīre) set against the main verb na hanyate.

ambiguities.topic: Whose self is this — the self that is Brahman, the individual self, or the knower of the Lord?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the self asked about in 1.2.14 and pointed to by Om, now described directly: «अथेदानीं तस्योङ्कारालम्बनस्यात्मनः साक्षात्स्वरूपनिर्दिधारयिषयेदमुच्यते». Raṅgarāmānuja, following Vyāsārya: this verse and the next concern the individual self, «मन्त्रद्वयमपि जीवविषयकमेव», because no one imagines the Supreme as slayer or slain. Madhva: the Lord came from nowhere, and so his knower, the vipaścit, is not born and does not die: «अयं भगवान् कुतोऽपि न बभूव यस्मादतस्तद्वेत्तापि विपश्चिन्न जायते न म्रियते च».

Śaṅkara reads it as a separate statement: nothing other came from this self, «अस्माच्चात्मनो न बभूव कश्चिदर्थान्तरभूतः». Raṅgarāmānuja: it did not earlier become anyone, as a man or another being, «पूर्वमपि मनुष्यादिरूपेण जननशून्यः». Madhva: no individual self came to be of itself; it is ‘born’ through connection with a body, «देहसम्बन्धाद्धि जायते».
Madhva’s text ends the line hanyamāne ’pi dehe, ‘even when the body is slain’ (corrections.json, variant): another word for body, with api, the same count of syllables.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Regular: 22 and 22 syllables, four pādas of eleven.

beginner: Here Yama finally starts to answer the boy's question about what survives death. The real self, he says, is never born and never dies. It did not come from anything, and nothing is produced out of it. It is unborn, eternal, lasting and ancient, yet always new, as Śaṅkara puts it. When the body is struck and killed, the self is not killed. Śaṅkara compares it to space, which is never wounded by what happens to the things it fills. The great commentators disagree about whose self this is: the self that is one with the absolute, the individual soul, or the soul that knows God. But they all read the verse as a denial that death touches what we most truly are. The Bhagavad Gītā repeats almost the same words.
analogy: Like the space inside a jar: smash the jar and the space is not broken — it was never made of clay.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the knowing self is neither born nor dies, has no source and produces nothing, is unborn, eternal, lasting and ancient, and is not slain when the body is slain.

commentary.q: Why name birth and death first?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: of all the changes a produced thing undergoes, birth and death are the first and the last, so denying them denies every change: «तासामाद्यन्ते जन्मविनाशलक्षणे विक्रिये इहात्मनि प्रतिषिध्येते». Purāṇa means it is ‘new even of old’, «पुरापि नव एवेति», since it does not grow by parts; and it abides in the body unharmed, like space, «तत्स्थोऽप्याकाशवदेव».

commentary.q: Why does Raṅgarāmānuja take it of the individual self?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Because the next verse speaks of a slayer and a slain, and nobody thinks of the Supreme that way: «न हि परमात्मनि वध्यधातुकभावभ्रान्तिः कस्याप्यस्ति». Each adjective then gives a reason for a denial: unborn for ‘not born’, eternal for ‘does not die’, and so on. The Supreme is introduced only at 1.2.20.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse first concerns the Lord, who came from nowhere, and then the wise who know him: birth and death are the body’s, not theirs. «यतः कश्चिज्जीवः स्वतो न बभूव । देहसम्बन्धाद्धि जायते» — no individual self came into being of itself; it is born through connection with a body. He supports it with verses he cites without naming a source.

commentary.q: How does the line stand in Madhva’s text?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Madhva’s mūla reads hanyamāne ’pi dehe for hanyamāne śarīre (corrections.json). The Gītā’s form of the verse (2.20) has śarīre, as the base does.

advaita.text: This is the self beyond all change, the same as Brahman, which Om pointed to: «अथेदानीं तस्योङ्कारालम्बनस्यात्मनः साक्षात्स्वरूपनिर्दिधारयिषयेदमुच्यते». Since it has no birth or decay, it is not harmed by what happens to the body.

visistadvaita.text: The verse and the next describe the individual self, which is eternal and unborn: «मन्त्रद्वयमपि जीवविषयकमेव». The Supreme, whose body it is, is taught next, from 1.2.20.

dvaita.text: Because the Lord came from nowhere, his knower is not born and does not die: «अयं भगवान् कुतोऽपि न बभूव यस्मादतस्तद्वेत्तापि विपश्चिन्न जायते न म्रियते च». The individual self is born only through a body.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara reads one self, identical with Brahman; Raṅgarāmānuja reads the individual self, distinct from the Supreme of 1.2.20; Madhva reads the Lord and the soul who knows him. All three deny that death touches the self.

parallels.quote: अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे
parallels.note: The Gītā’s second line is the Kaṭha’s word for word; its first line differs (kadācin nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ).
The sūtra that the self is not produced. Raṅgarāmānuja, following the Śrībhāṣya, cites it with this verse (his reference numbers it 2.3.18 and reads nātmā śruteḥ).

contemporary.text: Most people meet death as the end of a story. The verse asks the reader to separate two questions that usually travel together: what happens to the body, and what happens to the one who knows. Whatever one believes, it is a useful distinction to hold at a bedside. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: When you say ‘I’, do you mean your body, your memories, or the one who is aware of both?
reflect.deeper: Why does Śaṅkara think that denying birth and death denies every other change?
reflect.practice: Notice one change in your body today, and ask what in you noticed it without changing.

references.text: Raṅgarāmānuja reports Vyāsārya and the Śrībhāṣya on Brahmasūtra 2.3; Madhva cites verses without naming their source. These are reported as cited by them.

flags.note: Whether the subject is the self identical with Brahman (Śaṅkara), the individual self (Raṅgarāmānuja) or the Lord’s knower (Madhva) decides how 1.2.18–25 hang together.
Madhva’s text reads hanyamāne ’pi dehe for hanyamāne śarīre (corrections.json).
